title: Historical Christianity: From Jesus of Nazareth to a Global Faith
description: A history of Christianity as historians tell it, for readers who know the outline and want the evidence and the arguments. It runs from the Judaism of the Second Temple and Jesus as a historical figure through the first churches, the creeds and councils, the parting of East and West, the medieval church and the Reformations, to a faith whose center now lies in Africa, Asia and Latin America. Every chapter works from primary sources and keeps a clear line between what historical method can establish and what Christians believe by faith. It aims to be fair to Orthodox, Catholic, Protestant and other Christians alike, and to the Jews and Muslims whose histories are entwined with theirs.
prerequisites: A general knowledge of world history, or the companion History of Religion (REL 101)
Willingness to read short primary sources in translation
objectives: Explain how historians work with religious sources, and separate historical claims from faith claims in any account of Christian origins.
Describe Second Temple Judaism and summarize what historians broadly agree about Jesus of Nazareth, with the sources behind each point.
Trace how Christian scripture, creeds and church offices took shape from Paul to the Council of Chalcedon (451).
Explain the causes and stages of the estrangement between the Eastern and Western churches, and the place of the Oriental Orthodox churches and the Church of the East.
Analyze the medieval Western church's institutions, reforms and conflicts, including crusade and inquisition, from primary sources.
Compare the Lutheran, Reformed, Radical, English and Catholic Reformations in their teaching and consequences.
Describe the growth of Christianity beyond Europe since 1500 and where Christians live today, with dated figures.
Read a primary source critically: date it, place it, identify its purpose, and say what it can and cannot show.

chapters.title: Second Temple Judaism and the Historian's Craft
chapters.summary: How historians study religious history, and the Jewish world into which Jesus was born.
chapters.challenge: Read 1 Maccabees 1 and a passage of the Community Rule from the Dead Sea Scrolls, and write a short source analysis of each: author, date, purpose, and what it shows about Judaism in the last two centuries BCE.

sections.summary: Sources, evidence and probability, and why historians set aside claims about the supernatural without denying them.

preface:
This book tells the history of Christianity the way historians tell it: from evidence, with dates, and with open arguments about what the evidence means. It is for readers who know the outline (Jesus, Paul, Constantine, Luther) and want to know how we know it, what is disputed, and how a small Jewish movement in first-century Judea became the faith of more than two billion people.

We start before Christianity, in the Judaism of the Second Temple, because neither Jesus nor Paul makes sense outside it. From there we follow the first churches, the councils that defined the creeds, the parting of East and West, the medieval church, the Reformations and the modern world, and we end where most Christians now live: in Africa, Latin America and Asia. Each chapter puts a primary source in your hands (a letter, a creed, a decree) and asks you to read it as a historian would.

Three things travel with us. The first is the Nicene Creed, which we watch being made, argued over and divided over, and which is still recited in the worship of most of the world's Christians. The second is the Lord's Supper, which Christians have celebrated and disputed in every century. The third is the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem: built by Constantine, destroyed and rebuilt, and shared today by several churches under a careful arrangement, so that its stones carry much of the story.

One rule runs through every page. History can tell you what Christians believed and why, what happened and what followed from it. It cannot tell you whether God raised Jesus from the dead, and neither will this book. I will be fair to every tradition, which sometimes means telling each of them something about its past that it would rather not hear.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as a historian of Christianity would, in the manner of MacCulloch, Chadwick and Pelikan: from primary sources read in context, archaeology and the best recent scholarship, neutral about the supernatural and equally fair to every Christian tradition and to Christianity's Jewish and Muslim neighbors.
bible.promise: By the last page you will be able to tell the story of Christianity from its Jewish origins to its global present, read its key documents as a historian, and explain how and why its traditions divided, without taking sides.
threads: Historical method and faith claims: what evidence can establish, and what it must leave to belief.
Unity and division: every chapter asks what held Christians together and what drove them apart.
Doctrine has a history: beliefs were argued out in particular places, languages and politics.
Christianity was never only European: the churches of Asia and Africa appear in every era, not just the last chapter.
Primary sources first: every chapter reads at least one document closely.

runningExamples.name: The Nicene Creed
runningExamples.use: From Paul's 'one Lord' (1 Corinthians 8:6) to Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381), the filioque quarrel between East and West, its retention by the Reformers, and its shared use today.

runningExamples.name: The Lord's Supper
runningExamples.use: Paul's account (1 Corinthians 11) and the Didache, medieval eucharistic doctrine and the Fourth Lateran Council (1215), the Reformation disputes (Marburg, 1529; Trent), and twentieth-century convergence.

runningExamples.name: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Jerusalem
runningExamples.use: One building across the whole story: Constantine's foundation, its destruction in 1009, crusader rebuilding, and the Status Quo arrangement among the churches that share it today.

conventions: Dates as BCE and CE; give the date of every council, reign and document at first mention (Council of Chalcedon, 451).
Call each church by the name it uses for itself (Orthodox, Catholic, Oriental Orthodox, Church of the East, Lutheran, Reformed, Anabaptist, Pentecostal), and note when a name began as an insult.
Report what councils condemned as heresy in their own words, and give the condemned parties' views from their own surviving writings where possible.
Every chapter quotes and analyzes at least one primary source, cited to a standard collection or translation (Bettenson and Maunder where possible).
Give statistics with source and year (for example, Pew Research Center, 2020 data).

Companion books: for what the Catholic Church teaches today in its own terms, and for the contents of the biblical books, point to Catholicism and the Bible (THE 101); for theories of religion, the Axial Age, and Judaism and Islam in their own right, point to History of Religion (REL 101). Do not re-teach them here.

bible.care: This is a history, not a theology, and it follows methodological neutrality: historians explain events by causes open to public evidence, so they neither affirm nor deny claims about God's action. Faith claims are reported as the beliefs of particular people, with their sources ('Paul writes that the risen Christ appeared to him'; 'the council taught that the Son is of one being with the Father'), while historical claims carry their evidence and a stated level of confidence (almost certain, probable, disputed). That Jesus existed and was crucified under Pilate is treated as the near-consensus it is among historians; the resurrection is treated as the disciples' belief, whose origins and effects historians study, not as an event history can confirm or rule out. Be fair to every tradition and to Jews and Muslims: tell Christian hostility to Jews, the crusades, inquisitions, wars of religion, and complicity in colonialism and slavery plainly, with careful numbers and ranges and without polemic, and equally refuse the caricatures one tradition has drawn of another. Where a church's own account of its history differs from historians' reconstruction (for example, on apostolic succession or a church's founding), give both and label each.
